problems.description: test_app.py: test classes use lowercase names instead of PascalCase.
test_app.py: module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE.

Whole service (websocket server, health endpoint, message protocol) lives in a single app.py; cognitive complexity +64 will make later story sessions harder to extend, so protocol/server/entry-point separation is worth planning.
Client registry is mutated from the asyncio loop under a threading.RLock; the snapshot property mitigates races, but the threading/async mix should be revisited as the service grows.

strengths: Shared NotificationServer instance keeps the HTTP health count always current, with rationale documented in the module docstring
clients property returns a defensive snapshot, encapsulating the mutable registry
Timezone-aware UTC timestamps and message-type validation (SUPPORTED_TYPES) make the protocol robust
Clean typing with from __future__ import annotations; zero bugs, zero duplications, 0.88 convention score
Consistent internal patterns: snake_case functions, PascalCase class, UPPER_CASE constants
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, coherent greenfield replacement of the seed with an async WebSocket notification server, held back only by minor test-file naming violations and rising single-file complexity.

problems.description: test_app.py: Classes should use PascalCase
test_app.py: Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE

New /channels/{name}/subscribers HTTP endpoint exposes raw client IDs over the wire; client_id values are also emitted in direct-message routing, so assess whether these are sensitive before exposing externally

strengths: Channel-based pub/sub extends the existing protocol cleanly via SUPPORTED_TYPES and make_message with a defaulted channel arg, preserving backward compatibility
Subscription cleanup on disconnect prevents stale/orphaned channel entries
channels property returns defensive snapshots (copied sets) under the lock, consistent with existing thread-safety style
HTTP path parsing hardened with urlsplit/unquote instead of raw string splitting
SonarQube metrics improved: smells -6, cognitive complexity -50, no new bugs or duplications

problems.description: _store_message executes a synchronous SQLite write inside the asyncio event loop (called from _publish_or_deliver without offloading); the blocking call can stall the loop during a burst of broadcasts.
__init__ now performs I/O (sqlite3.connect, CREATE TABLE, commit), making construction heavier and harder to test/inject; connection setup would fit better in an explicit open/start lifecycle step.
_deliver performs an awaited Redis smembers round-trip on every broadcast delivery hot path when Redis is enabled; subscriber sets could be cached locally.
Redis publish failures in _publish_or_deliver are not caught (only the _redis_listener loop guards exceptions), so a Redis outage during send/broadcast would propagate unhandled to callers.
Cognitive complexity rose +46 in _deliver due to nested channel/client branch logic; SonarQube reports 0 smells so it stays under thresholds, but the branching could be decomposed.

strengths: Dual-mode design routes through _publish_or_deliver and degrades cleanly to local delivery when Redis is absent, preserving existing single-instance behavior.
Graceful lifecycle management: redis task cancellation, pubsub/redis close, and sqlite close are all handled in close(), plus redis cleanup on error.
Correct thread-safety for the shared SQLite connection via RLock and check_same_thread=False.
Centralizing delivery logic into _deliver removes duplication between broadcast and send_direct while keeping the existing make_message/LOGGER conventions intact.
Publishing to Redis without a local _deliver on the same instance avoids double-delivery in the fan-out path.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured integration that adds Redis pub/sub fan-out and SQLite persistence behind a clean single-writer abstraction with proper lifecycle and thread-safety, matching the measured 0.88 convention score with only minor event-loop and reliability nits.

problems.description: The clients property now returns self.transport.clients directly instead of a snapshot copy, contradicting its own docstring ('never the mutable registry'); unless the transport returns a copy, callers can observe the live registry mid-mutation.

Client registry ownership is split: app.py guards reads with self._clients_lock while transport.py mutates the registry in async callbacks outside that lock, so synchronization of the registry and _subscriptions is no longer centralized.
clients property type is weakened from dict[str, ServerConnection] to dict[str, Any], losing the connection type information that static analysis previously had.
New transport.py contributes +7 smells and +187 cognitive complexity per SonarQube; worth keeping the abstraction thin so the app.py simplification isn't offset.
The 2 convention violations (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE constants) are reported in test_app.py, which is not touched by this diff; they appear pre-existing rather than introduced by this commit.

strengths: Clean BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport abstraction with constructor injection and env-var fallback, matching the existing config pattern (DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL)
Lifecycle (start/stop/wait_closed) and per-client send logic centralized into the transport, shrinking NotificationServer responsibilities
Subscription cleanup consolidated into a dedicated _client_disconnected handler, removing the tangled try/except/finally in _websocket_handler
Enables alternate transports (e.g. SSE, unix sockets) and simplifies unit testing via the injected transport parameter
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally sound transport extraction that simplifies NotificationServer and improves testability, but splits client-registry ownership in a way that introduces a minor locking/snapshot concern.

problems.description: The /messages vs /history split is inlined inside the monolithic HTTP handler as a deep if/else chain, driving cognitive complexity +18; should be extracted into per-endpoint handler methods.
Cleanup interval is hardcoded to 3600s while rate_limit and message_ttl_days are env-configurable; the interval should follow the same _env_int pattern.
Local rate-counter fallback duplicates the Redis bucket logic rather than sharing it, so the two paths can drift.
_cleanup_expired_messages and the counter pruning perform synchronous sqlite/dict work on the event loop, consistent with the pre-existing pattern but potentially blocking.
Convention violations in test_app.py (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE module constants); note the shown diff is app.py-only, the +1 AST file implies the test changes carry these.

strengths: Redis minute-bucket rate limiting via INCR + EXPIRE with a graceful local fallback when Redis is absent.
Cleanup task lifecycle mirrors the existing _redis_task start/stop pattern with proper CancelledError handling.
limit+1 'has_more' pagination for /history is a clean, composable design that pairs naturally with TTL-based cleanup.
Env-driven configuration through the _env_int helper stays consistent with the existing DATABASE_URL/TRANSPORT env pattern.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive commit that adds rate limiting, message TTL cleanup, and time-based history pagination while reusing existing Redis/async/env patterns, at the cost of deep inline branching in the HTTP handler and a hardcoded cleanup interval.

compounding_issues: Compiled __pycache__/*.pyc bytecode committed to git starting in Session 4 (and mutated again in Session 5), with no .gitignore ever added — pollutes history and causes checkout conflicts

Session 3 introduced blocking sqlite3.connect(check_same_thread=False) calls guarded by threading.RLock inside an asyncio server; this sync-in-async pattern persisted and Session 5 added more blocking DB work (TTL cleanup, channel history)
.instrument/session.jsonl churned in every commit, mixing experiment telemetry into project history

Transport abstraction arrived in Session 4, only after Session 3 had already wired WebSocket-specific and Redis delivery paths directly into NotificationServer — the refactor had to unwind that coupling, leaving the health handler still reaching into transport.clients
key_decisions: Single shared NotificationServer instance serving both WebSocket and HTTP health/listener endpoints (Session 1)
Channel subscription model via subscribe/unsubscribe protocol messages with per-channel delivery filtering (Session 2)
Redis pub/sub backbone with per-channel subscriber sets and client presence keys for multi-instance delivery, with graceful local fallback when Redis is absent (Session 3)
SQLite message persistence enabling /messages and /history retrieval endpoints (Session 3)
Pluggable BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport abstraction selected via env TRANSPORT var (Session 4)
Redis-or-local dual-path design carried through rate limiting, subscriptions, and delivery so the server runs without Redis (Sessions 3, 5)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. Session 1 produced a functional WebSocket/health server (2 tests); Session 2 cleanly extended the protocol with channels and subscriptions (4 tests); Session 3 was the largest jump, adding Redis multi-instance delivery and SQLite persistence with history endpoints (6 tests); Session 4 refactored the WebSocket layer behind a transport abstraction without regressing the existing 6-test surface; and Session 5 hardened the system with cross-cutting operational features — Redis-aware rate limiting, message TTL cleanup, and paginated channel history (8 tests). All sessions remained green, with each feature layering on the preceding commit's abstractions rather than reworking them.
story_review.summary: A textbook-coherent progression from greenfield server through protocol features, integration, refactor, and operational hardening — quality rose steadily and tests stayed green throughout, only marred by committed bytecode artifacts and a sync-in-async persistence pattern.
